title: Transactions
subtitle: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, and ACID guarantees
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: A bank transfer requires two operations: debit one account, credit another. If the debit succeeds but the app crashes before the credit, money disappears. You need 'all or nothing' semantics.
whyItExists.solution: A transaction groups multiple statements into an atomic unit. Either all of them succeed (COMMIT) or all are undone (ROLLBACK). No partial state is ever visible.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any sequence of writes that must succeed or fail together: bank transfers, order placement (create order + update stock), user registration (insert user + create profile).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Single read-only queries don't need explicit transactions (though databases wrap them implicitly). Don't hold transactions open longer than needed — they hold locks.

explainModes.beginner: A transaction is an 'all or nothing' group of database operations. Like transferring money: you debit one account and credit another. If anything fails in between, you roll everything back to where you started — no money lost.
explainModes.simple: BEGIN; ... statements ... COMMIT; — wraps statements in a transaction. If error: ROLLBACK; undoes everything since BEGIN. Without BEGIN, each statement is its own auto-transaction. SAVEPOINT name; creates a checkpoint within a transaction. ROLLBACK TO name; rolls back to that point without undoing everything.
explainModes.standard: ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (constraints always satisfied), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crash). SQLite isolation: serialized by default — only one writer at a time. PostgreSQL: multiple isolation levels. BEGIN DEFERRED/IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE (SQLite) controls when locks are acquired. Nested transactions via savepoints.
explainModes.technical: Isolation levels (PostgreSQL): READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads), READ COMMITTED (default, no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no phantom reads after first read), SERIALIZABLE (fully serialized). Phantoms: new rows inserted by concurrent transaction that match your WHERE condition. SQLite is serializable by default. Transaction log (WAL) records uncommitted changes — on crash, incomplete transactions are rolled back during recovery.
explainModes.deepDive: MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control): instead of locking rows for reads, PostgreSQL keeps old row versions for concurrent readers. Writers create new versions; readers see the snapshot from their transaction start. This avoids read-write contention. Deadlock: T1 holds lock A waiting for B; T2 holds B waiting for A. PostgreSQL detects deadlocks and aborts one transaction. SQLite prevents deadlocks by serializing writes. Two-Phase Commit (2PC) for distributed transactions across multiple databases.

questions.question: What does ACID stand for in database transactions?
questions.explanation: ACID is the set of guarantees a transactional database provides: Atomicity (all statements in a transaction succeed or all fail), Consistency (constraints are never violated), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes), Durability (committed data survives crashes and restarts).

faq.q: Does every SQL statement run in a transaction?
faq.a: Yes — in SQLite and most databases, every statement that isn't explicitly wrapped in BEGIN...COMMIT is automatically wrapped in its own implicit transaction. This means a single UPDATE that updates 1000 rows is atomic by default. Explicit transactions let you group multiple statements into one atomic unit.

examples: BEGIN; INSERT INTO orders ...; UPDATE products SET stock=stock-qty WHERE id=?; COMMIT; — order + stock together
SAVEPOINT before_charge; ... charge card ... ; if fails: ROLLBACK TO before_charge — charge with fallback
Python: with conn: — automatically commits on success, rollbacks on exception
